title: LRU Cache Design
summary: Designing an O(1) get/put cache by pairing a hashmap with a doubly linked list — the hashmap makes lookup instant, the list makes recency order and eviction O(1).

slides.markdown:
LRU (Least Recently Used) Cache is a favorite design question because it forces you to compose two data structures, and neither one alone satisfies the contract. The requirement: `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` both in O(1), and when the cache is full, evict the item that hasn't been accessed in the longest time.

A plain hashmap gives O(1) lookup but has no concept of recency order. A plain linked list gives O(1) reordering (move a node to the front) but O(n) lookup to even find the node in the first place. Neither structure alone works — the design insight is pairing them: a hashmap of key to **node**, where each node lives inside a doubly linked list ordered by recency.

This topic is the payoff of the whole group — every earlier hashmap trick was about *what* the map stores; here the map's value is a pointer into a second structure entirely.

slides.sectionTitle: The requirement that rules out either structure alone
slides.markdown:
Write out the contract precisely, because the whole design falls out of it: `get(key)` returns the value in O(1) and marks the key as most-recently-used; `put(key, value)` inserts or updates in O(1), also marking it most-recently-used, and if the cache is at capacity, evicts the **least**-recently-used entry first.

A hashmap alone gives O(1) `get`/`put` by key, but has no way to answer "which key hasn't been touched in the longest time" without scanning every entry — O(n). A doubly linked list alone can track recency order perfectly (most-recent at the front, least-recent at the back) and move a node to the front in O(1) *once you have a reference to that node* — but finding the node for a given key in the first place is an O(n) list traversal.

Each structure solves exactly the half the other one is missing. That's the design move: use the hashmap purely to skip the list's O(n) search, and use the list purely to track what the hashmap can't.

slides.subTitle: Into a doubly linked list ordered by recency
slides.markdown:
The combined structure: a hashmap `key -> node`, where each node is also linked into a doubly linked list. The list is kept ordered by recency — most-recently-used at the **head**, least-recently-used at the **tail**. Two sentinel nodes (a dummy head and dummy tail) simplify every insert/remove by eliminating null-pointer special cases at the true ends.

![Keys A, B, C mapped to node boxes that are also linked in a doubly linked list from head (most recent) to tail (least recent)](assets/lru-map-and-list.svg)

assets.alt: Keys A, B, C mapped to node boxes that are also linked in a doubly linked list from head (most recent) to tail (least recent)

slides.subTitle: O(1) removal needs a back-pointer (see linked-lists)
slides.markdown:
Removing an arbitrary node from a **singly** linked list in O(1) is impossible if all you have is a reference to that node — you need the *previous* node to redirect its `next` pointer, and a singly linked list gives you no way to reach backward from a given node.

A **doubly** linked list solves this directly: every node already holds a `prev` pointer, so unlinking a node is `node.prev.next = node.next` and `node.next.prev = node.prev` — both O(1), no traversal needed to find the previous node. This is exactly why LRU Cache requires a doubly linked list specifically, not just "a linked list": the `get`/`put` operations need to move an arbitrary node to the front, and move-to-front is really "remove from current position, then insert at head" — removal is the step that needs the back-pointer.

slides.subTitle: Hashmap lookup, then move the node to the front
slides.markdown:
```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, value):
        self.key, self.value = key, value
        self.prev = self.next = None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.map = {}                      # key -> Node
        self.head = Node(None, None)       # dummy, most-recent side
        self.tail = Node(None, None)       # dummy, least-recent side
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def _remove(self, node):
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev

    def _insert_at_front(self, node):
        node.next = self.head.next
        node.prev = self.head
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.map:
            return -1
        node = self.map[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._insert_at_front(node)
        return node.value
```

`get` is two O(1) steps: the hashmap gives instant access to the node (skipping any list search entirely), then the node moves to the front to record that it was just used — a remove and a re-insert, both O(1) because the doubly linked list needs no traversal to unlink an already-located node.

slides.subTitle: Insert-or-update, then evict the tail on overflow
slides.markdown:
```python
    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.map:
            node = self.map[key]
            node.value = value
            self._remove(node)
            self._insert_at_front(node)
            return
        if len(self.map) >= self.capacity:
            lru = self.tail.prev
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.map[lru.key]
        node = Node(key, value)
        self.map[key] = node
        self._insert_at_front(node)
```

Three branches, each O(1): key already exists — update its value and move it to the front, same as a touch; cache is full — remove the node just before the tail sentinel (the true least-recently-used entry) from both the list and the map; otherwise — create a fresh node, register it in the map, and insert it at the front. The eviction step is exactly why the map and list must stay in sync: forgetting `del self.map[lru.key]` leaves a dangling map entry pointing at a node no longer in the list.

slides.subTitle: Capacity exceeded, tail node unlinked from both structures
slides.markdown:
Capacity 2, current state: map `{A, B}`, list `head -> B -> A -> tail` (B most-recent). Now `put("C", ...)` arrives: capacity is full, so the node just before the tail sentinel — A — is identified as the true least-recently-used entry.

Eviction is two coordinated removals, not one: unlink A from the doubly linked list (`_remove`), **and** delete A's entry from the hashmap. Do only the first and the map still claims A exists, returning a stale hit on `get("A")`. Do only the second and the list still holds a now-unreachable-by-map node, silently wasting memory and corrupting recency order for anything that later touches it.

![Before and after put of C, showing A removed from both the linked list and the map as the least-recently-used entry](assets/lru-eviction-walkthrough.svg)

assets.alt: Before and after put of C, showing A removed from both the linked list and the map as the least-recently-used entry

slides.sectionTitle: Updating one structure, forgetting the other
slides.markdown:
The single most common bug in an LRU Cache implementation: mutating the linked list without mutating the hashmap in the same step, or the reverse. Because the two structures are only correct **together**, every operation that touches one must touch the other in the same breath.

Concrete failure modes: evicting a node from the list but forgetting `del self.map[key]` leaves a hashmap entry pointing at an orphaned node — `get` on that key returns a value for something that's supposed to be gone. Updating a node's value on `put` for an existing key but forgetting to move it to the front leaves stale recency order, so a genuinely-just-used key can be evicted as if it were old.

The defensive habit: write `_remove`/`_insert_at_front` as the *only* ways any code touches the list, and make every hashmap mutation happen adjacent to the matching list mutation in the same method — never let one drift without the other in the same commit of logic.

slides.subTitle: Recency vs frequency, and LFU's second frequency map
slides.markdown:
| | LRU (Least Recently Used) | LFU (Least Frequently Used) |
|---|---|---|
| Evicts | The entry not accessed in the longest time | The entry accessed the fewest total times |
| Core structures | Hashmap + one doubly linked list | Hashmap + a second map from frequency to a list of keys at that frequency |
| get/put complexity | O(1) | O(1), but with meaningfully more bookkeeping |
| Good for | Access patterns with temporal locality (recent = likely to reuse) | Access patterns where some keys are consistently hot regardless of recency |

LFU needs an extra layer: a map from **frequency count** to a doubly linked list of all keys currently at that frequency, plus tracking the current minimum frequency, so that eviction can jump straight to the lowest-frequency bucket instead of scanning for it. Every access bumps a key's frequency and moves it from one frequency-bucket's list to the next — genuinely more moving parts than LRU's single list, which is why LRU is the default choice unless the workload specifically has "some keys are always hot" behavior that recency alone doesn't capture.

slides.subTitle: Evicting before vs after the new insert
slides.markdown:
A subtle bug: checking capacity **after** inserting the new node instead of before, which either lets the cache briefly exceed capacity or evicts the wrong entry.

The correct order for `put` on a new key: check `len(self.map) >= self.capacity` **first**, evict if so, **then** insert the new node. Insert first and check after, and a cache at capacity 2 can momentarily hold 3 entries before eviction catches up — and if the eviction logic then removes "the tail," it might remove the entry you just inserted (if it landed at the tail somehow) instead of the genuinely oldest one.

The reliable pattern: always make room *before* adding something new, never add-then-clean-up. This is the same class of bug as an array resize that grows *after* an overflowing write instead of before it — the fix is always to check the invariant before the operation that could violate it, not after.

The dummy head and tail nodes aren't just a convenience — they eliminate an entire category of null-pointer edge cases that a "real head/tail can be None" design forces you to handle everywhere.

Without sentinels, inserting into an empty list needs a special branch ("is this the first node? then set both head and tail to it"), and removing the only remaining node needs another ("did we just remove the last real node? then reset head/tail to None"). With two permanent dummy nodes that are never removed, `_remove` and `_insert_at_front` are unconditional — they always have a real `prev`/`next` to relink to, even when the list is otherwise empty.

This is a general pattern worth carrying beyond LRU Cache: sentinel/dummy nodes at the boundaries of a linked structure routinely turn "three special cases plus the general case" into just the general case, at the cost of two nodes' worth of constant memory.

slides.sectionTitle: Language shortcuts, and when to still explain the mechanism
The pattern this group ends on
slides.markdown:
LRU Cache is the clearest example in this entire group of hashmaps solving half a problem and needing a partner structure for the other half. Every earlier topic used a hashmap alone because the other half of the problem was just "count," "group," or "look up a complement" — simple enough for the map to carry unassisted. Here, tracking *order* is fundamentally something a hashmap cannot do, and the doubly linked list is the structure built exactly for reordering in O(1).

The transferable design instinct: when a problem needs both fast key-based lookup **and** some ordering property a hashmap alone can't express (recency, priority, insertion order under mutation), look for the structure that owns that ordering property natively, and use the hashmap purely to eliminate that structure's usual search cost. That's LRU Cache with a linked list, and it's the same shape behind a hashmap paired with a heap for a priority-aware cache, or a hashmap paired with a balanced tree for an order-statistics structure.
